welcome: Welcome, and thank you for joining us to celebrate this special day. We are honored to begin this new chapter surrounded by the people we love most.
Hindu wedding ceremonies are rich with symbolism and rooted in ancient Vedic traditions and philosophy that date back thousands of years.
We've created this program to guide you through each ritual and its significance. Our hope is that it helps you follow along, stay engaged, and experience the ceremony on a deeper level.
Our ceremony will last approximately three hours, so get comfortable. By the end, you’ll not only witness a marriage, but also earn bragging rights for completing the full experience.
Enjoy the journey, and thank you for being part of it.
draftMessage: A preview of our ceremony program. We’re still refining the details.

events.title: The Mandap
paragraphs: The ceremonial altar is called the mandap, a sacred space where the wedding will take place, symbolizing the universe and cosmos. As the couple enters the mandap, they symbolically step away from the outside world and into a space where they will build their marriage.

For this reason, the parents from both sides are seated near the pillars, symbolizing their guidance and foundational support as the couple begins this new chapter. By standing under these four “pillars,” the couple acknowledges that their new family is built directly upon the strength and blessings of their lineage.

events.title: Vishnu and Lakshmi
paragraphs: A key concept in Hindu tradition is the relationship between Lord Vishnu and Goddess Lakshmi.

Vishnu represents preservation, protection, balance, and the sustaining force that maintains harmony in the universe. Lakshmi, the goddess of prosperity, abundance, beauty, and good fortune, is often depicted beside him.

They are often viewed as an ideal model of marriage. Their relationship reflects the values couples are encouraged to carry into married life: mutual respect, devotion, patience, compassion, and shared responsibility.
For this reason, newly married couples are compared aspirationally to Vishnu and Lakshmi, and encouraged to uphold their values.

The groom represents Lord Vishnu. This association is interpreted as aspirational: the groom is encouraged to embody the traits that Lord Vishnu champions (responsibility, stability, compassion, and care for his future family).

Brides are often symbolically associated with Goddess Lakshmi. Lakshmi represents a form of wealth that extends beyond material possessions—qualities such as sincerity, compassion, self-control, and contentment.

events.title: The Groom’s Entrance
paragraphs: The groom's arrival marks the beginning of the wedding ceremony.
On the morning of the wedding, grooms will typically embark on a journey to the bride’s home accompanied by family and friends.
By his side is his Saibala, a younger boy who serves as a symbolic guardian.
Traditionally dressed identically to the groom, the Saibala is seen as a younger reflection of him. This beautiful tradition symbolizes the passage through life’s stages.
We are delighted to have our nephew, Avery, honor this tradition as the Saibala and accompany the groom on this special day.

events.title: Var Puja
paragraphs: Hindu philosophy teaches that every person is considered divine in nature. Welcoming another person is seen as honoring the divine within them.

For this reason, the groom is received with traditional gestures of hospitality, including the washing of his feet, hands, and face, symbolizing respect, humility, and purification before entering the sacred space of marriage. He is then offered a seat.

Kuśa grass is placed on the seat prior to the groom sitting down. It is considered pure and sacred in Vedic tradition. By sitting on the kuśa grass, the groom becomes grounded and ready to start the ceremony.
He is then offered madhuparka, a traditional welcoming drink made of honey (sweetness), yogurt (nourishment), and ghee (purity). He is invited to taste it three times.

Afterwards, he is offered a leaf containing rice, flowers, and money which he holds in his palms, symbolizing his acceptance of blessings. Together, these offerings represent a shared wish for a prosperous and supported married life.

events.title: Kanya Aagman — The Bride’s Entrance
paragraphs: After the groom has been formally welcomed, the bride then makes her entrance.
Adorned with symbols of protection and prosperity, her arrival symbolizes warmth and light entering a new home, as well as new beginnings, with two lives and two journeys uniting as one.
As the bride enters, she carries the sacred conch, a symbol of purity, auspiciousness, and divine blessing.
The conch has long been used to announce sacred beginnings. Its presence marks this moment as a threshold—a passage from one chapter of her life into another.
As she carries it forward, she brings with her the blessings of the past, the love of the family that raised her, and the promise of the life she is about to create.
The conch reminds us that this is not simply an entrance into a ceremony, but the beginning of a new chapter in her journey.

events.title: Kanyadaan
paragraphs: In Sanskrit, kanya means "daughter," and daan means "gift" or "offering." While the ritual is often translated as "giving away the bride," many families understand it more deeply as an act of love, trust, and blessing rather than one of ownership.

In Hindu tradition, the birth of a daughter is often regarded as an extraordinary blessing. She is seen as bringing love, light, prosperity, and grace into the home, and is frequently associated with the qualities of Goddess Lakshmi.

During this ritual, the bride's father gently places his daughter's hand into the groom's while sacred mantras are recited by the priest. Beside them, the bride's brother pours holy water over their joined hands, symbolizing the family's blessings flowing into this new chapter.
The father entrusts the groom to cherish, honor, and walk beside his daughter throughout their journey together.
"Take care of her heart, for from this day forward, it becomes part of yours—and yours, part of hers."
In return, the groom promises to never fail his daughter. The primary prayer said during this ritual is divided into two parts: the father’s declaration and the groom’s assurance.

events.title: Tying the Knot
paragraphs: The bride’s shawl and the groom’s scarf are tied together by the eldest daughter in law using betel nuts and rice.
From this moment forward, many of the rituals are performed together, symbolizing that the couple now moves through life as partners.
Rice is a staple food in many parts of the world, so it naturally represents nourishment, prosperity, and abundance.

Because betel nuts are hard, long-lasting, and don't spoil easily, they are seen as a symbol of stability and endurance. Their strength and longevity serve as a wish that the marriage remain resilient through every season of life.

events.title: Ganesh Puja (Prayer)
paragraphs: Every meaningful journey begins by clearing the path ahead—and, perhaps more importantly, the path within.
For this reason, Hindu ceremonies traditionally begin by honoring Ganesha, who is regarded as the remover of obstacles and the patron of new beginnings.
Vedic philosophy teaches that some of life’s greatest obstacles come not from the world around us, but from within: desire, ego, anger, greed, attachment, pride, and jealousy.

As two individuals begin married life, they begin the journey from “I” to “we.” Each has spent a lifetime learning to think, choose, and live as an individual. Marriage asks them to look beyond the self and make space for another person’s needs and feelings.

The six inner obstacles remind us that this transition is not always easy. Desire can make us focus only on what we want; anger can prevent us from listening; pride can make it difficult to admit when we are wrong; and attachment, greed, and jealousy can create distance where there should be trust and understanding.

Marriage is the lifelong practice of recognizing these obstacles within ourselves and learning to move beyond them—not perfectly, but together. In doing so, “I” becomes “we,” and two individual lives become one shared journey.

events.title: Agni Pradīpan — Lighting the Sacred Fire
paragraphs: At the center of the mandap, the sacred fire, Agni, becomes the witness to the vows and promises made today. Fire symbolizes purity and transformation—it consumes what is offered and transforms it into something new. At the same time, it symbolically burns away impurities, leaving behind only what endures.

As offerings are placed into the fire, “Svaha” is spoken, meaning “I offer this.” Following each offering, “Idam Na Mama” is recited, meaning “This is not mine.” Together, they express the willingness to give without attachment and to release the ego.
Each offering carries its own symbolism:
Ghee represents clarity of intellect
Samagri (herbs) represents the cleansing of negative thoughts.
Grains represent growth and transformation
As the offerings disappear into the flames, they symbolize letting go of anger, greed, pride, fear, and attachment—making space for greater wisdom, love, and understanding.

For the bride and groom, Agni offers a powerful reminder that marriage is a journey of transformation: letting go of “I” and embracing “we,” growing beyond the selves they once knew and choosing to build something stronger together.

events.title: Mangal Pheras — The Seven Sacred Circles
paragraphs: As they walk around the sacred fire, they are beginning a journey, which represents walking through the cycles of time, space, and the creation of their new shared reality.

For the first four rounds, the bride leads. Her rounds represent that she has traveled through many stages, from the innocence of childhood, adolescence, and into the fullness of adulthood. According to the Vedas, the bride's journey is accompanied by divine guardianship, symbols of forces that accompany her as she grows and moves from one stage of life to the next, shaping the woman she is today. She steps forward into this new chapter with her own strength, wisdom, and grace.
After the fourth round, she arrives at the threshold of marriage.
For the final three, the groom then leads which represents that he accepts the responsibility of walking beside her, supporting and protecting her.

As they alternate leading the rounds, the ritual reflects a simple truth about every partnership: there will be moments when one partner leads, moments when the other does, and many more when they simply walk side by side.
They represent the beautiful passage from childhood to adulthood and ultimately from two individual journeys into one shared journey.
The circle has no beginning and no end. It evokes the cycles of life—the passing of seasons, the turning of years, and the changes that come with age.

And the journey is not only through one lifetime. In the Hindu understanding of life as a continuing spiritual journey, marriage can therefore be understood as two souls meeting again on that greater journey, walking together through this life and, in the deepest spiritual sense, continuing their journey across lifetimes.

events.title: The Offering of Parched Rice
paragraphs: During the sacred circles, the parched rice prepared earlier that morning by the mothers is offered into the sacred fire.

If you remember from the beginning of our journey, the mothers carefully sorted the grains at daybreak, setting aside only the best ones as a blessing for a marriage that would be strong, enduring, and prosperous.

Now, those same grains are offered into Agni, carrying with them the hopes, prayers, and blessings with which they were first prepared. What began as a quiet act of love before sunrise now becomes part of the ceremony itself.

As the parched rice is transformed by the sacred fire, it beautifully echoes one of the ceremony's central themes: that love grows through transformation. Just as the fire refines what is placed within it, marriage invites two people to be continually shaped by patience, compassion, and shared purpose throughout their lives together.

events.title: Saptapadi — The Seven Steps
paragraphs: Saptapadi literally means “seven steps.”

Walking side by side, the bride and groom take seven deliberate steps together, each representing a shared prayer. Together, the couple steps into married life side by side — not ahead of one another, not behind one another, but alongside one another.
According to the Vedas, the Saptapadi is the defining moment of the marriage. With the completion of the seventh step, the marriage is considered complete.
The seven distinct linear steps (Saptapadi) are believed to transition the couple out of the stage of youth and education and step them directly into the stage of householding and creation.

events.title: The Seven Vows
paragraphs:
Nourishment
May we provide for one another and build a home filled with warmth and care.

Strength
May we support one another in moments of challenge and growth.

Prosperity
May we work together toward abundance, purpose, and stability.

Family
May we honor our families, traditions, and the love that brought us here.

Future & Family
May we nurture those who come after us with kindness, wisdom, and compassion.

Health
May we protect one another’s well-being and walk through life in harmony.

Friendship
May we remain not only partners in marriage, but best friends for life.

events.title: Surya Puja (Sun Prayer)
paragraphs: Prayers are offered to Surya, the Sun, a symbol of light, life, and divine energy in Hindu tradition.

As the source of warmth and nourishment for all living beings, Surya represents vitality and clarity. Through this prayer, the bride and groom seek blessings for a marriage filled with health and the wisdom to navigate life together.

Across many ancient civilizations—including those of India, Egypt, Mesopotamia, and the Americas—the sun was deeply revered because it sustains all life on Earth. Without its light and energy, nothing could grow or survive. In Hindu tradition, honoring the sun is more about expressing gratitude for the life, order, and energy it makes possible. It is a reminder to recognize and appreciate the forces that quietly sustain us every day.

events.title: Touching the heart of the Bride
paragraphs: The groom symbolically acknowledges the bride’s heart—a gesture of recognition.

The promise first spoken during Kanyadaan is now reflected in a simple gesture. The groom places his hand upon the bride’s heart, symbolizing that her joys, burdens, and hopes have now become his own.
It reflects that marriage is not about hierarchy or ownership, but about two individuals choosing to see and understand one another deeply as equal partners in life.
By touching the heart, they are promising to completely synchronize their thoughts, feelings, and intentions so that they never operate out of selfish individuality again.

events.title: The Shift to the Heart (Union of Stillness and Energy)
paragraphs: The bride now moves to the groom’s left side, traditionally considered closer to his heart.
This position is regarded as one of closeness and honor, symbolizing emotional unity and the intention to walk through life in deep awareness of one another.

In Hindu philosophy, this moment reflects the union of complementary qualities — strength and compassion, stability and warmth, individuality and togetherness — coming into harmony as one shared life.

In this moment, the groom represents stillness/stability, while the bride represents energy/warmth. As she moves toward him while he remains still, the ritual reflects the meeting of these complementary forces in harmony.
In Hindu philosophy, this balance is often expressed through the idea that consciousness without energy is inert, while energy without consciousness lacks direction; together, they create wholeness.

events.title: Sindoor Daan
paragraphs: The groom applies Sindoor, a red powder, along the parting of the bride’s hair — a deeply intimate moment in Hindu marriage traditions.
The color red represents love, strength, protection, and devotion.

In this gesture, it also reflects a quiet vow of care, respect, responsibility within the relationship, and the honoring of the bride as a source of strength, presence, and partnership in life’s journey.
Fun Fact: The earliest evidence of sindoor dates back over 5,000 years to the Indus Valley Civilization (c. 3300–1300 BCE).

events.title: Exchange of Wedding Rings (Modern Addition)
paragraphs: The exchange of wedding rings is not originally part of Vedic rituals, but has become a common feature in modern Hindu weddings, influenced by global traditions and cultural exchange.
The couple faces each other at the mandap, where rings are often blessed with prayers or flowers before being exchanged.
Our nephew, Avery, has agreed to take on a double role today and serve as our ring bearer.

events.title: Mangalsutra
paragraphs: The mangalsutra is a necklace given by the groom to the bride during the wedding ceremony, symbolizing unity and lifelong commitment.

Traditionally made of gold and interspersed with black beads, it is worn close to the heart as a daily reminder that marriage is not built in a single moment, but through thousands of small acts of devotion over a lifetime.

In some interpretations, elements of the mangalsutra are also understood through complementary principles: gold symbolizes endurance and prosperity. The black beads are traditionally believed to protect the couple from negative energy and symbolize balance and grounding. Some philosophical readings also interpret this balance as reflecting the harmony of complementary energies, with gold representing the feminine energy (the bride) and the black beads representing the masculine energy (the groom) within a marriage.
It is important to note that meanings can vary across regions, families, and traditions — there is no single fixed interpretation.

events.title: Varmala — The Exchange of Garlands
paragraphs: The couple exchanges floral garlands, symbolizing mutual acceptance.
Derived from the Sanskrit words var (groom) and mala (garland), literally refers to “the garland of the groom.”
The tradition is also connected to the practice of Swayamvara, where a bride would choose her partner by placing a garland around his neck — a gesture of agency, honor, and choice.

events.title: Vidaai & Grihapravesh — Farewell and Welcome
paragraphs: Vidaai (farewell), the bride bids farewell to her childhood home, traditionally tossing rice behind her as a blessing of gratitude and prosperity for the family who raised her.
As the couple departs, they are welcomed by the groom’s mother in Grihapravesh, symbolizing warmth, acceptance, and the bride’s arrival into her new home.

thanks: Enjoy the journey, and thank you for being part of it.
